       III.       ROUTE 891 QUANTITATIVELY OUTPERFORMS OTHER ROUTES
                             RECOMMENDED IN INITIAL BRIEFING

        The Applicants,9 Staff,10 OPUC,11 and many Intervenors12 acknowledge that “there is no

mathematical formula” for route selection13 and that “no one factor controls or is dispositive.”14

As former Chairman Smitherman testified, route selection is “a balancing of factors,”15 and

Commission Staff’s witness Mr. Poole similarly confirmed that his recommendation was based

on professional judgment, not a mathematical formula, and acknowledged that “another qualified

engineer reviewing the same data could reasonably reach a different conclusion.”16 The Sneeds

agree with this framing. A holistic, judgment-based analysis of the record confirms that Route

891 is the superior choice, and the Initial Briefs filed by other parties fail to identify any route that

matches its combination of paralleling of property boundaries, protection of sensitive river

watersheds, low cost, and manageable habitable structure impacts.

         Route 891 outperforms all routes of interest on this factor. PUCT Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B)

requires the Commission to specifically consider the degree to which a proposed route follows

property lines.35 This is a critical routing criterion because it minimizes the intrusiveness into

Texas landowners’ real property rights, best preserves the existing highest and best use of the

property, minimizes the damages to property, and assists in consolidating infrastructure along

property lines.36 As this method serves to group visual and environmental impacts into a single,

centralized zone, the Commission also often views the extent to which a route parallels property

lines as a proxy for its impacts to community and aesthetic values.37

              2. Staff’s Paralleling Analysis for Route 487 Supports Route 891 When Properly
                 Weighted.

        Staff’s routing recommendation places undue weight on the utilization of existing

compatible rights-of-way as a proxy for minimizing landowner impact. While Staff highlights that

Route 487 parallels or utilizes compatible rights-of-way for approximately 49.64% of its length,46

this metric conflates two fundamentally different concepts: following corridors that already exist

versus following the natural boundaries that define landowner properties. Existing transmission

lines and roadways that qualify as “compatible rights-of-way” under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

frequently bisect ranches and tracts, cutting across the interior of properties rather than running

along their edges. Routing along these existing corridors does not minimize intrusion on individual

landowners; it simply layers a new overly severe intrusion on top of an existing one. For example,

        C. Route 891 Provides a Greater Buffer Zone for the Lampasas and San Saba
           Rivers Than All Other Routes of Interest.

        Some Initial Briefs support routes other than Route 891 on the basis of impacts to rivers

and waterways, focusing on river crossings and aggregate riparian mileage statistics from the

Environmental Assessment.52 That approach misses the critical point: when it comes to protecting

sensitive river watersheds, the location and distance of the line in relation to the river and

immediate tributaries matter far more than the total number of miles crossed.53

        Route 891 provides a greater buffer zone for both the Lampasas River and the San Saba

River than any other route of interest.54 The Applicants’ Proposed Route, through Links G13 and

G51, parallels stretches of the Lampasas River and crosses the Rocky Creek and Mill Creek

tributaries at particularly sensitive locations near their confluences with the Lampasas River, where

contaminants from transmission corridor disturbance have the shortest distance to travel before

reaching the river and the least opportunity for natural filtration.55 Route 891’s more southerly

alignment avoids both the paralleling and the sensitive tributary crossings, providing a materially

greater buffer for the watershed.56
